entries.c48fdb90766b0e80644dcfe21c4f9b14a9786a6a: <div sID="gen6839" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="15" osisID="1Kgs.15" sID="1Kgs.15"/> <div eID="gen6839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6840" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6841" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have an abstract of the history, I. Of two of the kings of Judah, Abijam, the days of whose reign were few and evil (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.1-1Kgs.15.8">ver. 1-8</reference>), and Asa, who reigned well and long, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.9-1Kgs.15.24">ver. 9-24</reference>. II. Of two of the kings of Israel, Nadab the son of Jeroboam, and Baasha the destroyer of Jeroboam's house, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.25-1Kgs.15.34">ver. 25-34</reference>.
entries.93e4c61c730f90875808d75b62cc4aaba45cf23c: <div eID="gen6841" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6840" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Abijam's Reign. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 958.)</title> <div sID="gen6842" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now in the eighteenth year of king Jeroboam the son of Nebat reigned Abijam over Judah. <hi type="super">2</hi> Three years reigned he in Jerusalem. And his mother's name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Maachah, the daughter of Abishalom. <hi type="super">3</hi> And he walked in all the sins of his father, which he had done before him: and his heart was not perfect with the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> his God, as the heart of David his father. <hi type="super">4</hi> Nevertheless for David's sake did the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> his God give him a lamp in Jerusalem, to set up his son after him, and to establish Jerusalem: <hi type="super">5</hi> Because David did <hi type="italic">that which was</hi> right in the eyes of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and turned not aside from any <hi type="italic">thing</hi> that he commanded him all the days of his life, save only in the matter of Uriah the Hittite. <hi type="super">6</hi> And there was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam all the days of his life. <hi type="super">7</hi> Now the rest of the acts of Abijam, and all that he did, <hi type="italic">are</hi> they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah? And there was war between Abijam and Jeroboam. <hi type="super">8</hi> And Abijam slept with his fathers; and they buried him in the city of David: and Asa his son reigned in his stead. <div eID="gen6842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6843" type="x-p"/> We have here a short account of the short reign of Abijam the son of Rehoboam king of Judah. He makes a better figure, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.1-2Chr.13.22">2 Chron. xiii.</reference>, where we have an account of his war with Jeroboam, the speech which he made before the armies engaged, and the wonderful victory he obtained by the help of God. There he is called <hi type="italic">Abijah—My father is the Lord,</hi> because no wickedness is there laid to his charge. But here, where we are told of his faults, <hi type="italic">Jah,</hi> the name of God, is, in disgrace to him, taken away from his name, and he is called <hi type="italic">Abijam.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Jer.22.24">Jer. xxii. 24</reference>. <div eID="gen6843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6844" type="x-p"/> I. Few particulars are related concerning him. 1. Here began his reign in the beginning of Jeroboam's eighteenth year; for Rehoboam reigned but seventeen, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.21">ch. xiv. 21</reference>. Jeroboam indeed survived Rehoboam, but Rehoboam's Abijah lived to succeed him and to be a terror to Jeroboam, while Jeroboam's Abijah (whom we read of <reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.1">ch. xiv. 1</reference>) died before him. 2. He reigned scarcely three years, for he died before the end of Jeroboam's twentieth year, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.9">v. 9</reference>. Being made proud and secure by his great victory over Jeroboam (<reference osisRef="2Chr.13.21">2 Chron. xiii. 21</reference>), God cut him off, to make way for his son Asa, who would be a better man. 3. <hi type="italic">His mother's name was Maachah, the daughter of Abishalom,</hi> that is, Absalom, David's son, as I am the rather inclined to think because two other of Rehoboam's wives were his near relations (<reference osisRef="2Chr.11.18">2 Chron. xi. 18</reference>), one the daughter of Jerimoth, David's son, and another the daughter of Eliab, David's brother. He took warning by his father not to marry strangers; yet thought it below him to marry his subjects, except they were of the royal family. 4. He carried on his father's wars with Jeroboam. As there was continual war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam, not set battles (these were forbidden, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.24">ch. xii. 24</reference>), but frequent encounters, especially upon the borders, one making incursions and reprisals on the other, so there was between Abijam and Jeroboam (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.7">v. 7</reference>), till Jeroboam, with a great army, invaded him, and then Abijam, not being forbidden to act in his own defence, routed him, and weakened him, so that he compelled him to be quiet during the rest of his reign, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.20">2 Chron. xiii. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen6844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6845" type="x-p"/> II. But, in general, we are told, 1. That he was not like David, had no hearty affection for the ordinances of God, though, to serve his purpose against Jeroboam, he pleaded his possession of the temple and priesthood, as that upon which he valued himself, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.10-2Chr.13.12">2 Chron. xiii. 10-12</reference>. Many boast of their profession of godliness who are strangers to the power of it, and plead the truth of their religion who yet are not true to it. <hi type="italic">His heart was not perfect with the Lord his God.</hi> He seemed to have zeal, but he wanted sincerity; he began pretty well, but he fell off, and <hi type="italic">walked in all the sins of his father,</hi> followed his bad example, though he had seen the bad consequences of it. He that was all his days in war ought to have been so wise as to make and keep his peace with God, and not to make him his enemy, especially having found him so good a friend in his war with Jeroboam, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.18">2 Chron. xiii. 18</reference>. <hi type="italic">Let favour be shown to the wicked, yet will he not learn righteousness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.26.10">Isa. xxvi. 10</reference>. 2. That yet it was for David's sake that he was advanced, and continued upon the throne; it was <hi type="italic">for his sake</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.4-1Kgs.15.5">v. 4, 5</reference>) that God thus <hi type="italic">set up his son after him;</hi> not for his own sake, nor for the sake of his father, in whose steps he trod, <hi type="italic">but for the sake of David,</hi> whose example he would not follow. Note, It aggravates the sin of a degenerate seed that they fare the better for the piety of their ancestors and owe their blessings to it, and yet will not imitate it. They stand upon that ground, and yet despise it, and trample upon it, and unreasonably ridicule and oppose that which they enjoy the benefit of. The kingdom of Judah was supported, (1.) That David might have a lamp, pursuant to the divine ordination of <hi type="italic">a lamp for his anointed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.132.17">Ps. cxxxii. 17</reference>. (2.) That Jerusalem might be established, not only that the honours put upon it in David's and Solomon's time might be preserved to it, but that it might be reserved to the honours designed for it in after-times. The character here given of David is very great—<hi type="italic">that he did that which was right in the eyes of the Lord;</hi> but the exception is very remarkable—<hi type="italic">save only in the matter of Uriah,</hi> including both his murder and the debauching of his wife. That was a bad matter; it was a remaining blot upon his name, a bar in his escutcheon, and the reproach of it was not wiped away, though the guilt was. David was guilty of other faults, but they were nothing in comparison of that; yet even that being repented of, though it be mentioned for warning to others, did not prevail to throw him out of the covenant, nor to cut off the entail of the promise upon his seed.
entries.272dbbb23a4fcd8ab51b6ca4adec321bbe8c2c9b: <div eID="gen6845" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Asa's Reign. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 914.)</title> <div sID="gen6846" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> And in the twentieth year of Jeroboam king of Israel reigned Asa over Judah. <hi type="super">10</hi> And forty and one years reigned he in Jerusalem. And his mother's name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Maachah, the daughter of Abishalom. <hi type="super">11</hi> And Asa did <hi type="italic">that which was</hi> right in the eyes of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , as <hi type="italic">did</hi> David his father. <hi type="super">12</hi> And he took away the sodomites out of the land, and removed all the idols that his fathers had made. <hi type="super">13</hi> And also Maachah his mother, even her he removed from <hi type="italic">being</hi> queen, because she had made an idol in a grove; and Asa destroyed her idol, and burnt <hi type="italic">it</hi> by the brook Kidron. <hi type="super">14</hi> But the high places were not removed: nevertheless Asa's heart was perfect with the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> all his days. <hi type="super">15</hi> And he brought in the things which his father had dedicated, and the things which himself had dedicated, into the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , silver, and gold, and vessels. <hi type="super">16</hi> And there was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all their days. <hi type="super">17</hi> And Baasha king of Israel went up against Judah, and built Ramah, that he might not suffer any to go out or come in to Asa king of Judah. <hi type="super">18</hi> Then Asa took all the silver and the gold <hi type="italic">that were</hi> left in the treasures of the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and the treasures of the king's house, and delivered them into the hand of his servants: and king Asa sent them to Benhadad, the son of Tabrimon, the son of Hezion, king of Syria, that dwelt at Damascus, saying, <hi type="super">19</hi> <hi type="italic">There is</hi> a league between me and thee, <hi type="italic">and</hi> between my father and thy father: behold, I have sent unto thee a present of silver and gold; come and break thy league with Baasha king of Israel, that he may depart from me. <hi type="super">20</hi> So Benhadad hearkened unto king Asa, and sent the captains of the hosts which he had against the cities of Israel, and smote Ijon, and Dan, and Abel-beth-maachah, and all Cinneroth, with all the land of Naphtali. <hi type="super">21</hi> And it came to pass, when Baasha heard <hi type="italic">thereof,</hi> that he left off building of Ramah, and dwelt in Tirzah. <hi type="super">22</hi> Then king Asa made a proclamation throughout all Judah; none <hi type="italic">was</hi> exempted: and they took away the stones of Ramah, and the timber thereof, wherewith Baasha had builded; and king Asa built with them Geba of Benjamin, and Mizpah. <hi type="super">23</hi> The rest of all the acts of Asa, and all his might, and all that he did, and the cities which he built, <hi type="italic">are</hi> they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah? Nevertheless in the time of his old age he was diseased in his feet. <hi type="super">24</hi> And Asa slept with his fathers, and was buried with his fathers in the city of David his father: and Jehoshaphat his son reigned in his stead. <div eID="gen6846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6847" type="x-p"/> We have here a short account of the reign of Asa; we shall find a more copious history of it <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.1-2Chr.16.14">2 Chron. xiv., xv., and xvi.</reference> Here is, <div eID="gen6847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6848" type="x-p"/> I. The length of it: <hi type="italic">He reigned forty-one years in Jerusalem,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.10">v. 10</reference>. In the account we have of the kings of Judah we find the number of the good kings and the bad ones nearly equal; but then we may observe, to our comfort, that the reign of the good kings was generally long, but that of the bad kings short, the consideration of which will make the state of God's church not altogether so bad within that period as it appears at first sight. Length of days is in Wisdom's right hand. <hi type="italic">Honour thy father,</hi> much more thy heavenly Father, <hi type="italic">that thy days may be long.</hi> <div eID="gen6848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6849" type="x-p"/> II. The general good character of it (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Asa did that which was right in the eyes of the Lord,</hi> and that is right indeed which is so in God's eyes; those are approved whom he commends. He did <hi type="italic">as did David his father,</hi> kept close to God, and to his instituted worship, was hearty and zealous for that, which gave him this honourable character, that he was like David, though he was not a prophet, or psalmist, as David was. If we come up to the graces of those that have gone before us it will be our praise with God, though we come short of their gifts. Asa was like David, though he was neither such a conqueror nor such an author; for <hi type="italic">his heart was perfect with the Lord all his days</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.14">v. 14</reference>), that is, he was both cordial and constant in his religion. What he did for God he was sincere in, steady and uniform, and did it from a good principle, with a single eye to the glory of God. <div eID="gen6849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6850" type="x-p"/> III. The particular instances of Asa's piety. His times were times of reformation. For, <div eID="gen6850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6851" type="x-p"/> 1. He removed that which was evil. There reformation begins; and a great deal of work of that kind his hand found to do. For, though it was but twenty years after the death of Solomon that he began to reign, yet very gross corruption had spread far and taken deep root. Immorality he first struck at: <hi type="italic">He took away the sodomites out of the land,</hi> suppressed the brothels; for how can either prince or people prosper while those cages of unclean and filthy birds, more dangerous than pest-houses, are suffered to remain? Then he proceeded against idolatry: <hi type="italic">He removed all the idols,</hi> even those <hi type="italic">that his father had made,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.12">v. 12</reference>. His father having made them, he was the more concerned to remove them, that he might cut off the entail of the curse, and prevent the visiting of that iniquity upon him and his. Nay (which redounds much to his honour, and shows his heart was perfect with God), when he found idolatry in the court, he rooted it out thence, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.13">v. 13</reference>. When it appeared that Maachah his mother, or rather his grandmother (but called his <hi type="italic">mother</hi> because she had the educating of him in his childhood), had an idol in a grove, though she was his mother, his grandmother,—though, it is likely, she had a particular fondness for it,—though, being old, she could not live long to patronise it,—though she kept it for her own use only, yet he would by no means connive at her idolatry. Reformation must begin at home. Bad practices will never be suppressed in the country while they are supported in the court. Asa, in every thing else, will honour and respect his mother; he loves her well, but he loves God better, and (like the Levite, <reference osisRef="Deut.33.9">Deut. xxxiii. 9</reference>) readily forgets the relation when it comes in competition with his duty. If she be an idolater, (1.) Her idol shall be destroyed, publicly exposed to contempt, defaced, and burnt to ashes <hi type="italic">by the brook Kidron,</hi> on which, it is probable, he strewed the ashes, in imitation of Moses (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.20">Exod. xxxii. 20</reference>) and in token of his detestation of idolatry and his indignation at it wherever he found it. Let no remains of a court-idol appear. (2.) She shall be deposed, He removed her from being queen, or from the queen, that is, from conversing with his wife; he banished her from the court, and confined her to an obscure and private life. Those that have power are happy when thus they have hearts to use it well. <div eID="gen6851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6852" type="x-p"/> 2. He re-established that which was good (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.15">v. 15</reference>): He <hi type="italic">brought into the house of God the dedicated things</hi> which he himself had vowed out of the spoils of the Ethiopians he had conquered, and which his father had vowed, but lived not to bring in pursuant to his vow. We must not only cease to do evil, but learn to do well, not only cast away the idols of our iniquity, but dedicate ourselves and our all to God's honour and glory. When those who, in their infancy, were by baptism devoted to God, make it their own act and deed to join themselves to him and vigorously employ themselves in his service, this is bringing in the dedicated things which they and their fathers have dedicated: it is necessary justice—rendering to God the things that are his. <div eID="gen6852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6853" type="x-p"/> VI. The policy of his reign. He built cities himself, to encourage the increase of his people (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.23">v. 23</reference>) and to invite others to him by the conveniences of habitation; and he was very zealous to hinder Baasha from building Ramah, because he designed it for the cutting off of communication between his people and Jerusalem and to hinder those who in obedience to God would come to worship there. An enemy must by no means be suffered to fortify a frontier town. <div eID="gen6853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6854" type="x-p"/> V. The faults of his reign. In both the things for which he was praised he was found defective. The fairest characters are not without some <hi type="italic">but</hi> or other in them. 1. Did he take away the idols? That was well; <hi type="italic">but the high places were not removed</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.14">v. 14</reference>); therein his reformation fell short. He removed all images which were rivals with the true God or false representations of him; but the altars which were set up in high places, and to which those sacrifices were brought which should have been offered on the altar in the temple, those he suffered to stand, thinking there was no great harm in them, they having been used by good men before the temple was built, and being loth to disoblige the people, who had a kindness to them and were wedded to them both by custom and convenience; whereas in Judah and Benjamin, the only tribes under Asa's government which lay so near Jerusalem and the altars there, there was less pretence for them than in those tribes which lay more remote. They were against the law, which obliged them to worship <hi type="italic">at one place,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.12.11">Deut. xii. 11</reference>. They lessened men's esteem of the temple and the altars there, and were an open gap for idolatry to enter in at, while the people were so much addicted to it. It was not well that Asa, when his hand was in, did not remove these. <hi type="italic">Nevertheless his heart was perfect with the Lord.</hi> This affords us a comfortable note, That those may be found honest and upright with God, and be accepted of him, who yet, in some instances, come short of doing the good they might and should do. The perfection which is made the indispensable condition of the new covenant is not to be understood of sinlessness (then we were all undone), but sincerity. 2. Did he bring in the dedicated things? That was well; but he afterwards alienated the dedicated things, when he took the gold and silver out of the house of God and sent them as a bribe to Benhadad, to hire him to break his league with Baasha, and, by making an inroad upon his country, to give him a diversion from the building of Ramah, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.18-1Kgs.15.19">v. 18, 19</reference>. Here he sinned, (1.) In tempting Benhadad to break his league, and so to violate the public faith. If he did wrong in doing it, as certainly he did, Asa did wrong in persuading him to do it. (2.) In that he could not trust God, who had done so much for him, to free him out of this strait, without using such indirect means to help himself. (3.) In taking the gold out of the treasury of the temple, which was not to be made use of but on extraordinary occasions. The project succeeded. Benhadad made a descent upon the land of Israel, which obliged Baasha to retire with his whole force from Ramah (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.20-1Kgs.15.21">v. 20, 21</reference>), which gave Asa a fair opportunity to demolish his works there, and the timber and stones served him for the building of some cities of his own, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.22">v. 22</reference>. But, though the design prospered, we find it was displeasing to God; and though Asa valued himself upon the policy of it, and promised himself that it would effectually secure his peace, he was told by the prophet that he had done foolishly, and that <hi type="italic">thenceforth he should have wars;</hi> see <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.7-2Chr.16.9">2 Chron. xvi. 7-9</reference>. <div eID="gen6854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6855" type="x-p"/> VI. The troubles of his reign. For the most part he prospered; but, 1. Baasha king of Israel was a very troublesome neighbour to him. He reigned twenty-four years, and all his days had war, more or less, with Asa, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.16">v. 16</reference>. This was the effect of the division of the kingdoms, that they were continually vexing one another, and so weakened one another, which made them both an easier prey to the common enemy. 2. In his old age he was himself afflicted with the gout: He was <hi type="italic">diseased in his feet,</hi> which made him less fit for business and peevish towards those about him. <div eID="gen6855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6856" type="x-p"/> VII. The conclusion of his reign. The acts of it were more largely recorded in the common history (to which reference is here had, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.23">v. 23</reference>) than in this sacred one. He reigned long, but finished at last with honour, and left his throne to a successor no way inferior to him.
entries.6af5f40cffd614f1b8a63679906a6b58b1863122: <div eID="gen6856" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Reign of Nadab and Baasha. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 954.)</title> <div sID="gen6857" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> And Nadab the son of Jeroboam began to reign over Israel in the second year of Asa king of Judah, and reigned over Israel two years. <hi type="super">26</hi> And he did evil in the sight of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and walked in the way of his father, and in his sin wherewith he made Israel to sin. <hi type="super">27</hi> And Baasha the son of Ahijah, of the house of Issachar, conspired against him; and Baasha smote him at Gibbethon, which <hi type="italic">belonged</hi> to the Philistines; for Nadab and all Israel laid siege to Gibbethon. <hi type="super">28</hi> Even in the third year of Asa king of Judah did Baasha slay him, and reigned in his stead. <hi type="super">29</hi> And it came to pass, when he reigned, <hi type="italic">that</hi> he smote all the house of Jeroboam; he left not to Jeroboam any that breathed, until he had destroyed him, according unto the saying of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , which he spake by his servant Ahijah the Shilonite: <hi type="super">30</hi> Because of the sins of Jeroboam which he sinned, and which he made Israel sin, by his provocation wherewith he provoked the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel to anger. <hi type="super">31</hi> Now the rest of the acts of Nadab, and all that he did, <hi type="italic">are</hi> they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel? <hi type="super">32</hi> And there was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all their days. <hi type="super">33</hi> In the third year of Asa king of Judah began Baasha the son of Ahijah to reign over all Israel in Tirzah, twenty and four years. <hi type="super">34</hi> And he did evil in the sight of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and walked in the way of Jeroboam, and in his sin wherewith he made Israel to sin. <div eID="gen6857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6858" type="x-p"/> We are now to take a view of the miserable state of Israel, while the kingdom of Judah was happy under Asa's good government. It was threatened that they should be as <hi type="italic">a reed shaken in the water</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.15">ch. xiv. 15</reference>), and so they were, when, during the single reign of Asa, the government of their kingdom was in six or seven different hands, as we find in this and the following chapter. Jeroboam was upon the throne in the beginning of his reign and Ahab at the end of it, and between them were Nadab, Baasha, Elah, Zimri, Tibni, and Omri, undermining and destroying one another. This they got by deserting the house both of God and of David. Here we have, 1. The ruin and extirpation of the family of Jeroboam, according to the word of the Lord by Ahijah. His son Nadab succeeded him. If the death of his brother Abijah had had a due influence upon him to make him religious, and the honour done him at his death had engaged him to follow his good example, his reign might have been long and glorious; but he <hi type="italic">walked in the way of his father</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.26">v. 26</reference>), kept up the worship of his calves, and forbade his subjects to go up to Jerusalem to worship, <hi type="italic">sinned and made Israel to sin,</hi> and therefore God brought ruin upon him quickly, in the second year of his reign. He was besieging Gibbethon, a city which the Philistines had taken from the Danites, and was endeavouring to re-take it; and there, in the midst of his army, did Baasha, with others, conspire against him and kill him, (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.27">v. 27</reference>), and so little interest had he in the affections of his people that his army did not only not avenge his death, but chose his murderer for his successor. Whether Baasha did it upon a personal pique against Nadab, or to be avenged on the house of Jeroboam for some affront received from them, or whether under pretence of freeing his country from the tyranny of a bad prince, or whether merely from a principle of ambition, to make way for himself to the throne, does not appear; but he <hi type="italic">slew him</hi> and <hi type="italic">reigned in his stead,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.28">v. 28</reference>. And the first thing he did when he came to the crown was to <hi type="italic">cut off all the house of Jeroboam,</hi> that he might the better secure himself and his own usurped government. He thought it not enough to imprison or banish them, but he destroyed them, left not only no males (as was foretold, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.10">ch. xiv. 10</reference>), but none that breathed. Herein he was barbarous, but God was righteous. Jeroboam's sin was punished (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.30">v. 30</reference>); for those that provoke God do it <hi type="italic">to their own confusion;</hi> see <reference osisRef="Jer.7.19">Jer. vii. 19</reference>. Ahijah's prophecy was accomplished (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.29">v. 29</reference>); for no word of God shall fall to the ground. Divine threatenings are not bugbears. 2. The elevation of Baasha. He shall be tried awhile, as Jeroboam was. Twenty-four years he reigned (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.33">v. 33</reference>), but showed that it was not from any dislike to Jeroboam's sin that he destroyed his family, but from malice and ambition; for, when he had rooted out the sinner, he himself clave to the sin, and <hi type="italic">walked in the way of Jeroboam</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.34">v. 34</reference>), though he had seen the end of that way; so strangely was his heart hardened with the deceitfulness of sin.  <chapter eID="1Kgs.15"/> <div eID="gen6858" type="x-p"/>

entries.7e544e0262143fa15c9dc1245e2871d33a5bb88c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3244"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 15</title> <div sID="gen4539" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.1-1Kgs.15.8">1Ki 15:1-8</reference>. Abijam's Wicked Reign over Judah.<div eID="gen4539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4540" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3244"/><hi type="bold">1. Abijam--</hi>His name was at first Abijah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.12.16">2Ch 12:16</reference>); "Jah," the name of God, according to an ancient fashion, being conjoined with it. But afterwards, when he was found "walking in all the sins of his father" [1Ki 15:3], that honorable addition was withdrawn, and his name in sacred history changed into Abijam [Lightfoot]. <div eID="gen4540" type="x-p"/>
entries.7ed1cc3ee2ef3c2e770df59a0c0d31ea04bfd94a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3245"/><div sID="gen4541" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3245"/><hi type="bold">2. Three years reigned he--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.1">1Ki 15:1</reference> with <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.9">1Ki 15:9</reference>). Parts of years are often counted in Scripture as whole years. The reign began in Jeroboam's eighteenth year, continued till the nineteenth, and ended in the course of the twentieth.<div eID="gen4541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4542" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his mother's name was Maachah--</hi>or Michaiah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.13.2">2Ch 13:2</reference>), probably altered from the one to the other on her becoming queen, as was very common under a change of circumstances. She is called the daughter of Abishalom, or Absalom (<reference osisRef="2Chr.11.21">2Ch 11:21</reference>), of Uriel (<reference osisRef="2Chr.13.2">2Ch 13:2</reference>). Hence, it has been thought probable that Tamar, the daughter of Absalom (<reference osisRef="2Sam.14.27">2Sa 14:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.18.18">18:18</reference>), had been married to Uriel, and that Maachah was their daughter. <div eID="gen4542" type="x-p"/>
entries.f3c85d71b1b415126d5ff700fa40d9dc5abd1bf3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3246"/><div sID="gen4543" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3246"/><hi type="bold">3. his heart was not perfect with the Lord ... , as the heart of David his father--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.4">1Ki 11:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.22">14:22</reference>). He was not positively bad at first, for it appears that he had done something to restore the pillaged treasures of the temple (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.15">1Ki 15:15</reference>). This phrase contains a comparative reference to David's heart. His doing that which was right in the eyes of the Lord (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.5">1Ki 15:5</reference>) is frequently used in speaking of the kings of Judah, and means only that they did or did not do that which, in the general course and tendency of their government, was acceptable to God. It furnishes no evidence as to the lawfulness or piety of one specific act. <div eID="gen4543" type="x-p"/>
entries.be91242046f3ac6139f5da8f21ad6d90eb1358d7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3247"/><div sID="gen4544" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3247"/><hi type="bold">4. for David's sake did the Lord his God give him a lamp--</hi>"A lamp" in one's house is an Oriental phrase for continuance of family name and prosperity. Abijam was not rejected only in consequence of the divine promise to David (see on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.13-1Kgs.11.36">1Ki 11:13-36</reference>).<div eID="gen4544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4545" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.9-1Kgs.15.22">1Ki 15:9-22</reference>. Asa's Good Reign. <div eID="gen4545" type="x-p"/>
entries.7784aa2f0373d5f6d9e1600ec1931ac4588bc7fd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3248"/><div sID="gen4546" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3248"/><hi type="bold">10-13. his mother's name was Maachah--</hi>She was properly his grandmother, and she is here called "the king's mother," from the post of dignity which at the beginning of his reign she possessed. Asa, as a constitutional monarch, acted like the pious David, laboring to abolish the traces and polluting practices of idolatry, and in pursuance of his impartial conduct, he did not spare delinquents even of the highest rank. <div eID="gen4546" type="x-p"/>
entries.a890699e229a73b3db2efe604636cd8b7a748ab8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3250"/><div sID="gen4549" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3250"/><hi type="bold">15. he brought in the things which his father had dedicated--</hi>Probably the spoils which Abijam had taken from the vanquished army of Jeroboam (see <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.16">2Ch 13:16</reference>).<div eID="gen4549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4550" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and the things which himself had dedicated--</hi>after his own victory over the Cushites (<reference osisRef="2Chr.14.12">2Ch 14:12</reference>). <div eID="gen4550" type="x-p"/>
entries.454105321e25a13556214ca93c7178dac58ddf59: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3251"/><div sID="gen4551" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3251"/><hi type="bold">16-17. there was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all their days--</hi>Asa enjoyed a ten years' peace after Jeroboam's defeat by Abijam, and this interval was wisely and energetically spent in making internal reforms, as well as increasing the means of national defense (<reference osisRef="2Chr.14.1-2Chr.14.7">2Ch 14:1-7</reference>). In the fifteenth year of his reign, however, the king of Israel commenced hostilities against him, and, invading his kingdom, erected a strong fortress at Ramah, which was near Gibeah, and only six Roman miles from Jerusalem. Afraid lest his subjects might quit his kingdom and return to the worship of their fathers, he wished to cut off all intercourse between the two nations. Ramah stood on an eminence overhanging a narrow ravine which separated Israel from Judah, and therefore he took up a hostile position in that place. <div eID="gen4551" type="x-p"/>
entries.1d837ae7ccbd0f99e182863245fc42ac1f02cddb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3252"/><div sID="gen4552" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3252"/><hi type="bold">18-20. Then Asa took all the silver and the gold that were left in the ... house of the Lord--</hi>Asa's religious character is now seen to decline. He trusted not in the Lord (<reference osisRef="2Chr.16.7">2Ch 16:7</reference>). In this emergency Asa solicited the powerful aid of the king of Damascene-Syria; and to bribe him to break off his alliance with Baasha, he transmitted to him the treasure lying in the temple and palace. The Syrian mercenaries were gained. Instances are to be found, both in the ancient and modern history of the East, of the violation of treaties equally sudden and unscrupulous, through the presentation of some tempting bribe. Ben-hadad poured an army into the northern provinces of Israel, and having captured some cities in Galilee, on the borders of Syria, compelled Baasha to withdraw from Ramah back within his own territories.<div eID="gen4552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4553" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ben-hadad--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.14">1Ki 11:14</reference>). <div eID="gen4553" type="x-p"/>
entries.0ce36c27411cd88013855986aa73045cbc2a1d6d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3253"/><div sID="gen4554" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3253"/><hi type="bold">22. Then king Asa made a proclamation--</hi>The fortifications which Baasha had erected at Ramah were demolished, and with the materials were built other defenses, where Asa thought they were needed--at Geba (now Jeba) and Mizpeh (now Neby Samuil), about two hours' travelling north of Jerusalem. <div eID="gen4554" type="x-p"/>
entries.bfedbaccc581eca005d1a6de5948c1a0b006d6d8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3254"/><div sID="gen4555" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3254"/><hi type="bold">23. in the time of his old age he was diseased in his feet--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.12">2Ch 16:12</reference>, where an additional proof is given of his religious degeneracy.)<div eID="gen4555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4556" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.25-1Kgs.15.34">1Ki 15:25-34</reference>. Nadab's Wicked Reign. <div eID="gen4556" type="x-p"/>
entries.dd284a37c24691a077a1b472ae3482131eba6dc4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3255"/><div sID="gen4557" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3255"/><hi type="bold">25. Nadab the son of Jeroboam began to reign--</hi>No record is given of him, except his close adherence to the bad policy of his father. <div eID="gen4557" type="x-p"/>
entries.30f376e887fc731dd3b4996cc708a241af8325dc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3256"/><div sID="gen4558" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3256"/><hi type="bold">27. Baasha smote him at Gibbethon--</hi>This town, within the tribe of Dan, was given to the Levites (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.44">Jos 19:44</reference>). It lay on the Philistine borders, and having been seized by that people, Nadab laid siege to recover it. <div eID="gen4558" type="x-p"/>
entries.6df57ac3350683fe1793c71662d7dc790cafcfd8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3257"/><div sID="gen4559" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3257"/><hi type="bold">29. when he reigned, he smote all the house of Jeroboam--</hi>It was according to a barbarous practice too common in the East, for a usurper to extirpate all rival candidates for the throne; but it was an accomplishment of Ahijah's prophecy concerning Jeroboam (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.10">1Ki 14:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.11">11</reference>). <chapter eID="1Kgs.15"/>

entries.8e2c91474c673d9099d88e17f08d0ddad41a6672: <div eID="gen12011" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen12012" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12013" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12013" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12012" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12014" type="x-p"/> Abijam's wicked reign, and death, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.1-1Kgs.15.8">1Kgs 15:1-8</reference>. Asa succeeds him in the kingdom of Judah, and rules well, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.9-1Kgs.15.15">1Kgs 15:9-15</reference>. He makes a league with the king of Syria against Baasha king of Israel, who is obliged to desist in his attempts against Judah, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.16-1Kgs.15.22">1Kgs 15:16-22</reference>. He is diseased in his feet and dies, and is succeeded by his son Jehoshaphat, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.23-1Kgs.15.25">1Kgs 15:23-25</reference>. Nadab, son of Jeroboam, reigns over Israel; but is slain by Baasha, who reigns in ha stead, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.26-1Kgs.15.28">1Kgs 15:26-28</reference>. Baasha destroys all the house of Jeroboam, according to the prediction of Ahijah, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.29">1Kgs 15:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.30">1Kgs 15:30</reference>. Baasha continues the idolatry of Jeroboam, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.31-1Kgs.15.34">1Kgs 15:31-34</reference>. <div eID="gen12014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12015" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen12015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12016" type="x-p"/> Reigned Abijam over Judah - Of this son of Rehoboam, of his brethren, and of Rehoboam's family in general, see 2 Chronicles 12, where many particulars are added.
entries.115e001336d82556bfabdfc99a270a560289d0c1: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen12016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12017" type="x-p"/> His heart was not perfect - He was an idolater, or did not support the worship of the true God. This appears to be the general meaning of the heart not being perfect with God.
entries.8975c508ada58c2345c8e0443bfcc281cbc9bf4b: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen12017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12018" type="x-p"/> The Lord - give him a lamp - That is, a son to succeed him; see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.36">1Kgs 11:36</reference>.
entries.6e7e6e32f54454117722986c3e1edd5bf12ca476: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen12018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12019" type="x-p"/> Save only in the matter of Uriah - Properly speaking, this is the only flagrant fault or crime in the life of David. It was a horrible offense, or rather a whole system of offenses. See the notes on 2 Samuel 11 (note), and 2 Samuel 12 (note).
entries.ea5768a88b3a875e826950c81f9ed5404a7bf160: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen12019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12020" type="x-p"/> There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam - This was mentioned in the preceding chapter, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.30">1Kgs 14:30</reference>, and it can mean no more than this: there was a continual spirit of hostility kept up between the two kingdoms, and no doubt frequent skirmishing between bordering parties; but it never broke out into open war, for this was particularly forbidden. See <reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.24">1Kgs 12:24</reference>. Hostility did exist, and no doubt frequent skirmishes; but open war and pitched battles there were none. <div eID="gen12020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12021" type="x-p"/> But why is this circumstance repeated, and the history of Abijam interrupted by the repetition? There is some reason to believe that Rehoboam is not the true reading, and that it should be Abijam: "Now there was war between Abijam and Jeroboam all the days of his life." And this is the reading of fourteen of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS. The Syriac has Abia the son of Rehoboam; the Arabic has Abijam. In the Septuagint the whole verse is omitted in the London Polyglot, but it is extant in those of Complutum and Antwerp. Some copies of the Targum have Abijam also, and the Editio Princeps of the Vulgate has Abia. This is doubtless the true reading, as we know there was a very memorable war between Abia and Jeroboam; see it particularly described <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.3">2Chr 13:3</reference> (note), etc.
entries.f76762c8c2b7dfe956db01b6b1f59978fc4e8b49: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen12021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12022" type="x-p"/> His mother's name - Our translators thought that grandmother was likely to be the meaning, and therefore have put it in the margin. <div eID="gen12022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12023" type="x-p"/> The daughter of Abishalom - She is called, says Calmet, the daughter of Absalom, according to the custom of the Scriptures, which give the name of daughter indifferently to the niece, the grand-daughter, and great grand-daughter.
entries.df4218de4c26c6ce3272ac1e9d8b7aa1e74b1e2e: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen12023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12024" type="x-p"/> The sodomites - הקדשים hakkedeshim; literally, the holy or consecrated ones. See on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.24">1Kgs 14:24</reference> (note).
entries.732f8506c6eb17f55837d48ce58dc3154e24853f: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen12024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12025" type="x-p"/> She had made an idol in a grove - The original word, מפלצת miphletseth, is variously understood. I shall give its different views in the versions: - "Besides, he removed his mother Maacha from being chief in the sacred rites of Priapus, and in his grove which she had consecrated." - Vulgate. "And Ana, [other copies Maacha], he removed from being governess, because she had made an assembly in her grove." - Septuagint. "Moreover, he deprived Maacha, his mother, of her own magnificence, because she had celebrated a solemnity to her own worship." - Syriac. "And even Maacha, his mother, he removed from the kingdom, because she had made an idol in a grove." - Chaldee. "Besides, he removed Maacha, his mother, from her kingdom, because she had made a high tree into an idol." - Arabic. "Also he removed Maacha, his mother, from the kingdom, because she had made a horrible statue; and our rabbins say that it was called מפלצת miphletseth, because מפליא ליצנותא maphli leytsanutha, it produced wonderful ridicule; for she made it ad instar membri virilis, and she used it daily." - Rabbi Solomon Jarchi. <div eID="gen12025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12026" type="x-p"/> From the whole, it is pretty evident that the image was a mere Priapus, or something of the same nature, and that Maachah had an assembly in the grove where this image was set up, and doubtless worshipped it with the most impure rites. What the Roman Priapus was I need not tell the learned reader; and as to the unlearned, it would not profit him to know. Maachah was most likely another Messalina; and Asa probably did for his mother what Claudius did for his wife.
entries.f5c53686274f44652cd1a4a96ea1948f6a118be1: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen12026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12027" type="x-p"/> The high places were not removed - He was not able to make a thorough reformation; this was reserved for his son Jehoshaphat. <div eID="gen12027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12028" type="x-p"/> Asa's heart was perfect - He worshipped the true God, and zealously promoted his service; see on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.3">1Kgs 15:3</reference> (note). And even the high places which he did not remove were probably those where the true God alone was worshipped; for that there were such high places the preceding history amply proves, and Jarchi intimates that these were places which individuals had erected for the worship of Jehovah.
entries.6efded4699774e7b8acd8514981ac9968d2f551f: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen12028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12029" type="x-p"/> Which his father had dedicated - On what account he and his father dedicated the things mentioned below, we know not; but it appears that Asa thought himself bound by the vow of his father.
entries.68570cc21a11a778ed5f1aa93ddd65c22a0dc352: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen12029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12030" type="x-p"/> There was war - That is, there was continual enmity; see on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.6">1Kgs 15:6</reference> (note). But there was no open war till the thirty-sixth year of Asa, when Baasha, king of Israel, began to build Ramah, that he might prevent all communication between Israel and Judah; see <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.19">2Chr 15:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.1">2Chr 16:1</reference>. But this does not agree with what is said here, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.8">1Kgs 16:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.9">1Kgs 16:9</reference>, that Elah, the son and successor of Baasha, was killed by Zimri, in the twenty-sixth year of the reign of Asa. Chronologers endeavor to reconcile this by saying that the years should be reckoned, not from the beginning of the reign of Asa, but from the separation of the kingdoms of Israel and Judah. It is most certain that Baasha could not make war upon Asa in the thirty-sixth year of his reign, when it is evident from this chapter that he was dead in the twenty-sixth year of that king. We must either adopt the mode of solution given by chronologists, or grant that there is a mistake in some of the numbers; most likely in the parallel places in Chronicles, but which we have no direct means of correcting. But the reader may compare <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.1">2Chr 14:1</reference>, with <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.10">2Chr 15:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.19">2Chr 15:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.1">2Chr 16:1</reference>.
entries.fb7238e19e49d6384b3d1427a4a0aff13547a545: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen12030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12031" type="x-p"/> And Baasha - built Ramah - As the word signifies a high place, what is here termed Ramah was probably a hill, (commanding a defile through which lay the principal road to Jerusalem), which Baasha fortified in order to prevent all intercourse with the kingdom of Judah, lest his subjects should cleave to the house of David. Ramah was about two leagues northward of Jerusalem.
entries.006438a0b0c0de428ea5fb0d3043df3528ca5ad2: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen12031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12032" type="x-p"/> Asa took all the silver - Shishak, king of Egypt, had not taken the whole, or there had been some treasures brought in since that time. <div eID="gen12032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12033" type="x-p"/> Ben-hadad - This was the grandson of Rezon, called here Hezion, who founded the kingdom of Damascus. See <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.23">1Kgs 11:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.24">1Kgs 11:24</reference>; and Calmet.
entries.825f74b3ac773a1ed9706fb7a0c6b998da2abc9d: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen12033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12034" type="x-p"/> There is a league between me and thee - Or, Let there be a league between me and thee; as there was between my father and thy father. There was no reason why Asa should have emptied his treasures at this time to procure the aid of the Syrian king; as it does not appear that there was any danger which himself could not have turned aside. He probably wished to destroy the kingdom of Israel; and to effect this purpose, even robbed the house of the Lord.
entries.df7dc0aafbff6980559d123ec60517c6d4b2c110: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen12034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12035" type="x-p"/> Ijon, and Dan, etc. - He appears to have attacked and taken those towns which constituted the principal strength of the kingdom of Israel.
entries.3f251cce4af99997da6ff5768a8f9c10a30b0e26: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen12035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12036" type="x-p"/> Dwelt in Tirzah - This seems to have been the royal city; see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.33">1Kgs 15:33</reference>, and <reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.17">1Kgs 14:17</reference>; and in this Baasha was probably obliged to shut himself up.
entries.01a3897f9d08cf58930807c32753be8e66419c8e: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen12036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12037" type="x-p"/> None was exempted - Every man was obliged to go and help to dismantle the fortress at Ramah which Baasha had built. This was a general levee en masse of the people: every one was obliged to lend a helping hand, as the state was then supposed to be in danger, and all exemptions necessarily ceased. This is a maxim of civil policy, Ubi adversus hostem muniendi sent limites, omnis immunitas cessat: "Where the boundaries are to be fortified against an enemy, then all exemptions cease.
entries.b5c2b45d197ee1575038725fdadf5a988ca8fe19: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen12037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12038" type="x-p"/> And the cities which he built - Such as Geba and Mizpah, which he built out of the spoils of Ramah. <div eID="gen12038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12039" type="x-p"/> He was diseased in his feet - Probably he had a strong rheumatic affection, or the gout. This took place in the thirty-ninth year of his reign, three years before his death; and it is said that he sought to physicians rather than to the Lord, <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.12">2Chr 16:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.13">2Chr 16:13</reference>.
entries.64f86506d3128ec5dc5558f4e803c33cfff5cf44: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen12039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12040" type="x-p"/> Asa slept with his fathers - Of his splendid and costly funeral we read <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.14">1Chr 16:14</reference>.
entries.918ce1af89b4a62e2ac289072dc7912d8d0ad59d: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen12040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12041" type="x-p"/> Nadab - began to reign over Israel - He began his reign in the second year of the reign of Asa, and reigned two years.
entries.006df912d0ebb10a87d05a33585b402a0fa0da9c: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen12041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12042" type="x-p"/> Smote him at Gabbethon - This was a city in the tribe of Dan, and generally in the possession of the Philistines.
entries.37ca40a4612f47f00b182a9708cdadc4aaaacc45: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen12042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12043" type="x-p"/> He smote all the house of Jeroboam - This was according to Ahijah's prophetic declaration; see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.10">1Kgs 14:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.14">1Kgs 14:14</reference>. Thus God made use of one wicked man to destroy another.
entries.dc9860dbebb59cb163e3df3584cc4e2cf541ce6c: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen12043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12044" type="x-p"/> There was war - See on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.16">1Kgs 15:16</reference> (note).
entries.7eb3baa2bdf032bf33795c70fd213b27f863cb11: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen12044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12045" type="x-p"/> Walked in the way of Jeroboam - The entail of iniquity cannot be cut off but by a thorough conversion of the soul to God; and of this, these bad kings seem to have had no adequate notion. The wicked followed the steps of the wicked, and became still more wicked; sin gathers strength by exercise and age.  <chapter eID="1Kgs.15"/> <div eID="gen12045" type="x-p"/>

entries.989722d0ae71f9d003167089acfe1929010a8c0d: 1Ki 15:1-2 <div eID="gen4977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4978" type="x-p"/> Reign of Abijam (cf., 2 Chron 13). - <hi type="italic">Abijam</hi> reigned three years, and his mother’s name was <hi type="italic">Maacah</hi>, daughter (i.e., grand-daughter) of Absalom. We have the same in <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.20-2Chr.11.21">2Ch 11:20-21</reference>; but in <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.2">2Ch 13:2</reference> she is called <hi type="italic">Michajahu</hi>, daughter of Uriel of Gibeah. If אבישׁלום was without doubt Absalom, the well-known son of David, as we may infer from the fact that this name does not occur again in the Old Testament in connection with any other person, since Absalom had only one daughter, viz., <hi type="italic">Thamar</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.14.27">2Sa 14:27</reference>), who was fifty years old when Solomon died, Maacah must have been a daughter of this Thamar, who had married Uriel of Gibeah, and therefore a grand-daughter of Absalom. This is sustained by Josephus (<hi type="italic">Ant</hi>. viii. 10, 1). The form of the name מיכיהוּ is probably an error in copying for מעכה, as the name is also written in <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.20">2Ch 11:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.21">2Ch 11:21</reference>, and not a different name, which Maacah assumed as queen, as Caspari supposes (<hi type="italic">Micha</hi>, p. 3, note 4).
entries.5db104b551be9c91376438e23036058081b2de5b: 1Ki 15:3-5 <div eID="gen4978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4979" type="x-p"/> Abijam walked as king in the footsteps of his father. Although he made presents to the temple (1Ki 15:15), his heart was not שׁלם, wholly or undividedly given to the Lord, like the heart of David (cf., 1Ki 11:4); but (כּי, after a previous negative) for David’s sake Jehovah had left him a light in Jerusalem, to set up his son after him and to let Jerusalem stand, because (אשׁר) David had done right in the eyes of God, etc., i.e., so that it was only for David’s sake that Jehovah did not reject him, and allowed the throne to pass to his son. For the fact itself compare 1Ki 11:13, 1Ki 11:36; and for the words, “except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite,” see 2 Sam 11 and 12.
entries.face264e5973591e6aab1b8bcbb5453b36117010: 1Ki 15:6-8 “And there was war between <hi type="italic">Rehoboam</hi> and Jeroboam all his life;” i.e., the state of hostility which had already existed between Rehoboam and Jeroboam continued “all the days of his life,” or so long as Abijam lived and reigned. If we take חיּיו כּל־ימי in this manner (not כּל־ימיהם, 1Ki 15:16), the statement loses the strangeness which it has at first sight, and harmonizes very well with that in 1Ki 15:7, that there was also war between Abijam and Jeroboam. Under Abijam it assumed the form of a serious war, in which Jeroboam sustained a great defeat (see 2 Chron 13:3-20). - The other notices concerning Abijam in 1Ki 15:7, 1Ki 15:8 are the same as in the case of Rehoboam in 1Ki 14:29, 1Ki 14:31.
entries.366e233cc8084b2e18ffb1b2a9ff800808ee86a9: 1Ki 15:9 <div eID="gen4979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4980" type="x-p"/> Reign of Asa (cf., 2 Chron 14-16). - As Asa ascended the throne in the twentieth year of the reign of Jeroboam, his father Abijam, who began to reign in the eighteenth year of Jeroboam (1Ki 15:1), can only have reigned two years and a few months, and not three full years.
entries.43e323185d1cc8145be69f512366edd17a4eaa07: 1Ki 15:10 <div eID="gen4980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4981" type="x-p"/> Asa reigned forty-one years. “The name of his mother was Maacah, the daughter of Absalom.” This notice, which agrees verbatim with 1Ki 15:2, cannot mean that Abijam had his own mother for a wife; though Thenius finds this meaning in the passage, and then proceeds to build up conjectures concerning emendations of the text. We must rather explain it, as Ephr. Syr., the Rabbins, and others have done, as signifying that Maacah, the mother of Abijam, continued during Asa’s reign to retain the post of queen-mother or הגּבירה, i.e., sultana valide, till Asa deposed her on account of her idolatry (1Ki 15:13), probably because Asa’s own mother had died at an early age.
entries.ac80faea6f2411ab8dc0c240180e06dce1bf0ee3: 1Ki 15:11-14 <div eID="gen4981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4982" type="x-p"/> As ruler Asa walked in the ways of his pious ancestor David: he banished the male prostitutes out of the land, abolished all the abominations of idolatry, which his fathers (Abijam and Rehoboam) had introduced, deposed his grandmother Maacah from the rank of a queen, because she had made herself an idol for the Ashera, and had the idol hewn in pieces and burned in the valley of the Kidron. גּלּלים is a contemptuous epithet applied to idols (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.30">Lev 26:30</reference>); it does not mean <hi type="italic">stercorei</hi>, however, as the Rabbins affirm, but logs, from גּלל, to roll, or masses of stone, after the Chaldee גּלל (Ezr 5:8; Ezr 6:4), generally connected with שׁקּצים. It is so in Deu 29:16. מפלצת, <hi type="italic">formido</hi>, from פּלץ, <hi type="italic">terrere</hi>, <hi type="italic">timere</hi>, hence an idol as an object of fear, and not <hi type="italic">pudendum</hi>, a shameful image, as Movers (<hi type="italic">Phöniz</hi>. i. p. 571), who follows the Rabbins, explains it, understanding thereby a Phallus as a symbol of the generative and fructifying power of nature. With regard to the character of this idol, nothing further can be determined than that it was of wood, and possibly a wooden column like the אשׁרים (see at 1Ki 14:23). “But the high places departed not,” i.e., were not abolished. By the בּמות we are not to understand, according to 1Ki 15:12, altars of high places dedicated to idols, but unlawful altars to Jehovah. It is so in the other passages in which this formula recurs (1Ki 22:24; 2Ki 12:4; 2Ki 14:4; 2Ki 15:4; and the parallel passages <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.17">2Ch 15:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.33">2Ch 20:33</reference>). The apparent discrepancy between the last-mentioned passages and <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.2">2Ch 14:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.4">2Ch 14:4</reference>, and <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.6">2Ch 17:6</reference>, may be solved very simply on the supposition that the kings (Asa and Jehoshaphat) did indeed abolish the altars on the high places, but did not carry their reforms in the nation thoroughly out; and not by distinguishing between the <hi type="italic">bamoth</hi> dedicated to Jehovah and those dedicated to idols, as Thenius, Bertheau, and Caspari, with many of the earlier commentators, suppose. For although <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.2">2Ch 14:2</reference> is very favourable to this solution, since both בּמות and הגּכר dna בּמו מזבּחות are mentioned there, it does not accord with <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.6">2Ch 17:6</reference>, where הבּמות cannot be merely idolatrous altars dedicated to the Canaanitish Baal, but unquestionably refer to the unlawful altars of Jehovah, or at any rate include them. Moreover, the next clause in the passage before us, “nevertheless Asa’s heart was wholly given to the Lord,” shows that the expression סרוּ לא סרוּ nois does not mean that the king allowed the unlawful Jehovah-<hi type="italic">bamoth</hi> to remain, but simply that, notwithstanding his fidelity to Jehovah, the <hi type="italic">bamoth</hi> did not depart, so that he was unable to carry the abolition of them thoroughly out.
entries.bb270cf2acfc3a07fdbc9752e2947547f7ea6f0b: 1Ki 15:15 <div eID="gen4982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4983" type="x-p"/> He brought the sacred offerings of his father and his own sacred offerings into the house of Jehovah; probably the booty, in silver, gold, and vessels, which his father Abijam had gathered in the war with Jeroboam (<reference osisRef="2Chr.13.16-2Chr.13.17">2Ch 13:16-17</reference>), and he himself on the conquest of the Cushites (<reference osisRef="2Chr.14.12-2Chr.14.13">2Ch 14:12-13</reference>). The <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> וקדשׁי is a bad emendation of the correct reading in the <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> קדשׁו, i.e., קדשׁו (קדשׁיו); for יהוה בּית is an accusative, and is to be connected with ויּבא.
entries.fca7071d3069f69f529029b67e8638d71b04e9fa: 1Ki 15:16-17 <div eID="gen4983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4984" type="x-p"/> The state of hostility between Judah and Israel continued during the reign of Asa; and Baasha the king of Israel advanced, etc. These statements are completed and elucidated by the Chronicles. After the great victory obtained by Abijam over Jeroboam, the kingdom of Judah enjoyed rest for ten years (<reference osisRef="2Chr.14.1">2Ch 14:1</reference>). Asa employed this time in exterminating idolatry, fortifying different cities, and equipping his army (<reference osisRef="2Chr.14.1-2Chr.14.7">2Ch 14:1-7</reference>). Then the Cushite <hi type="italic">Zerah</hi> invaded the land of Judah with an innumerable army (in the eleventh year of Asa), but was totally defeated by the help of the Lord (<reference osisRef="2Chr.14.8-2Chr.14.14">2Ch 14:8-14</reference>); whereupon Asa, encouraged by the prophet Azariah, the son of Oded, proceeded with fresh zeal to the extermination of such traces of idolatry as still remained in the kingdom, then renewed the altar of burnt-offering in front of the temple-hall, and in the fifteenth year of his reign held, with the whole nation, a great festival of thanksgiving and rejoicing to the Lord at Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.1-2Chr.15.15">2Ch 15:1-15</reference>). The next year, the sixteenth of his reign and the thirty-sixth from the division of the kingdom (<reference osisRef="2Chr.16.1">2Ch 16:1</reference>), Baasha commenced hostilities, by advancing against Judah, taking possession of <hi type="italic">Ramah</hi>, the present <hi type="italic">er Râm</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.18.25">Jos 18:25</reference>), which was only two hours and a quarter from Jerusalem, and fortifying it. The occupation of Ramah is not expressly mentioned indeed, but it is implied in יהוּדה על ויּעל על יה, which affirms the hostile invasion of Judah. For Ramah, from its very situation in the heart of the tribe of Benjamin and the immediate neighbourhood of Jerusalem, can neither have been a border city nor have belonged to the kingdom of Israel. The intention of Baasha, therefore, in fortifying Ramah cannot have been merely to restrain his own subjects from passing over into the kingdom of Judah, but was evidently to cut off from the kingdom of Judah all free communication with the north. וגו תּת לבלתּי, “that they might not give one going out or one coming in to Asa;” i.e., to cut off from the others all connection with Asa, and at the same time to cut off from those with Asa all connection with this side. The main road from Jerusalem to the north passed by Ramah, so that by shutting up this road the line of communication of the kingdom of Judah was of necessity greatly disturbed. Moreover, the fortification of Ramah by Baasha presupposes the reconquest of the cities which Abijam had taken from the kingdom of Israel (<reference osisRef="2Chr.13.19">2Ch 13:19</reference>), and which, according to <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.19">2Ch 13:19</reference>, were still in the possession of Asa.
entries.7fd1fbc1a2aa14573f51f781ec50d5f8cc8c3b49: 1Ki 15:18-19 <div eID="gen4984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4985" type="x-p"/> In order to avert the danger with which his kingdom was threatened, Asa endeavoured to induce the Syrian king, Benhadad of Damascus, to break the treaty which he had concluded with Baasha and to become his ally, by sending him such treasures as were left in the temple and palace.<note placement="foot">Asa had sought help from the Lord and obtained it, when the powerful army of the Cushites invaded the land; but when an invasion of the Israelites took place, he sought help from the Syrians. This alteration in his conduct may probably be explained in part from the fact, that notwithstanding the victory, his army had been considerably weakened by the battle which he fought with the Cushites (<reference osisRef="2Chr.14.9">2Ch 14:9</reference>), although this by no means justified his want of confidence in the power of the Lord, and still less his harsh and unjust treatment of the prophet Hanani, whom he caused to be put in the house of the stocks on account of his condemnation of the confidence which he placed in the Syrians instead of Jehovah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.16.7-2Chr.16.10">2Ch 16:7-10</reference>).</note> הגּותרים may be explained from the face that the temple and palace treasures had been plundered by Shishak in the reign of Rehoboam (1Ki 14:26); and therefore what Asa had replaced in the temple treasury (1Ki 15:15), and had collected together for his palace, was only a remnant in comparison with the former state of these treasures. The name בּן־הדד, i.e., son of <hi type="italic">Hadad</hi>, the sun-god (according to Macrobius, i. 23; cf., Movers, <hi type="italic">Phöniz</hi>. i. p. 196), was borne by three kings of Damascus: the one here named, his son in the time of Ahab (1Ki 20:1, 1Ki 20:34), and the son of Hazael (2Ki 13:24). The first was a son of <hi type="italic">Tabrimmon</hi> and grandson of <hi type="italic">Hezyon</hi>. According to 1Ki 15:19, his father <hi type="italic">Tabrimmon</hi> (good is <hi type="italic">Rimmon</hi>; see at 2Ki 5:18) had also been king, and was the contemporary of Abijam. But that his grandfather <hi type="italic">Hezyon</hi> was also king, and the same person as the <hi type="italic">Rezon</hi> mentioned in 1Ki 11:23, cannot be shown to be even probable, since there is no ground for the assumption that Hezyon also bore the name Rezon, and is called by the latter name here and by the former in 1Ki 11:23.
entries.b0d4c8f3fb013eca3b81d9855b11a0f4f6e906de: 1Ki 15:20 <div eID="gen4985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4986" type="x-p"/> Benhadad consented to Asa’s request, and directed his captains to advance into the kingdom of Israel: they took several cities in the north of the land, whereby Baasha was compelled to give up fortifying Ramah and withdraw to Thirza. <hi type="italic">Ijon</hi> (עיּון) is to be sought for in all probability in Tell<hi type="italic">Dibbin</hi>, on the eastern border of <hi type="italic">Merj Ayun</hi>; and in <hi type="italic">Ajun</hi>, although Ajun is written with <hi type="italic">Aleph</hi>, the name <hi type="italic">Ijon</hi> is probably preserved, since the situation of this Tell seems thoroughly adapted for a fortress on the northern border of Israel (vid., Robinson, <hi type="italic">Bibl. Res</hi>. p. 375, and Van de Velde, <hi type="italic">Mem</hi>. p. 322). <hi type="italic">Dan</hi> is the present <hi type="italic">Tell el Kadi</hi>; see at Jos 19:47. <hi type="italic">Abel-Beth-Maachah</hi>, the present <hi type="italic">Abil el Kamh</hi>, to the north-west of Lake Huleh (see at <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.14">2Sa 20:14</reference>). “All <hi type="italic">Chinneroth</hi>” is the district of <hi type="italic">Chinnereth</hi>, the tract of land on the western shore of the Lake of Gennesareth (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.19.35">Jos 19:35</reference>). כּל־ארץ נ על, together with all the land of Naphtali (for this meaning of על fo gninaem  compare the Comm. on <reference osisRef="Gen.32.12">Gen 32:12</reference>). The cities named were the principal fortresses of the land of Naphtali, with which the whole of the country round was also smitten, i.e., laid waste.
entries.5f2ace80d74d1e4677be937785cfcdf73e3d3592: 1Ki 15:21 ויּשׁב, and remained at Thirza, his place of residence (see at 1Ki 14:17).
entries.a6d657082c01f66d022eebbd3230b997227ddda5: 1Ki 15:22 <div eID="gen4986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4987" type="x-p"/> Asa thereupon summoned all Judah נקי אין, <hi type="italic">nemine immuni</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">excepto</hi>, no one being free (cf., Ewald, §286, <hi type="italic">a</hi>.), and had the stones and the wood carried away from Ramah, and <hi type="italic">Geba</hi> and <hi type="italic">Mizpah</hi> in Benjamin built, i.e., fortified, with them. <hi type="italic">Geba</hi> must not be confounded with <hi type="italic">Gibeah</hi> of Benjamin or Saul, but is the present <hi type="italic">Jeba</hi>, three-quarters of an hour to the north-east of Ramah (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.18.24">Jos 18:24</reference>). <hi type="italic">Mizpah</hi>, the present <hi type="italic">Nebi Samwil</hi>, about three-quarters of a geographical mile to the south-west of Ramah (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.18.26">Jos 18:26</reference>).
entries.26674f1d52a36dcb164323be631dad6e83b1413f: 1Ki 15:23-24 <div eID="gen4987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4988" type="x-p"/> Of the other acts of Asa, the building of cities refers to the building of fortifications mentioned in <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.5">2Ch 14:5</reference>-6. The disease in his feet in the time of his old age commenced, according to <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.12">2Ch 16:12</reference>, in the thirty-ninth year of his reign; and he sought help from the physicians, but not from the Lord; from which we may see, that the longer he lived the more he turned his heart away from the Lord (compare <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.10">2Ch 16:10</reference>).
entries.b005826d98e056444265c5178c61e7336ab93cba: 1Ki 15:25 <div eID="gen4988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4989" type="x-p"/> The Reign of Nadab lasted not quite two years, as he ascended the throne in the second year of Asa, and was slain in his third year.
entries.113cadbbd8951432a926ad26814e9a4a5c97b25c: 1Ki 15:26-31 <div eID="gen4989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4990" type="x-p"/> He walked in the ways of his father (Jeroboam) and in his sin, i.e., in the calf-worship introduced by Jeroboam (1Ki 12:28). When Nadab in the second year of his reign besieged Gibbethon, which the Philistines and occupied, Baasha the son of Ahijah, of the house, I the family or tribe, of Issachar, conspired against him and slew him, and after he became king exterminated the whole house of Jeroboam, without leaving a single soul, whereby the prediction of the prophet Ahijah (1Ki 14:10.) was fulfilled. <hi type="italic">Gibbethon</hi>, which was allotted to the Danites (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.44">Jos 19:44</reference>), has not yet been discovered. It probably stood close to the Philistian border, and was taken by the Philistines, from whom the Israelites attempted to wrest it by siege under both Nadab and Baasha (1Ki 16:16), though apparently without success. לא השׁאיר כּל־נשׁמה as in <reference osisRef="Josh.11.14">Jos 11:14</reference> (see the Comm. on <reference osisRef="Deut.20.16">Deu 20:16</reference>).
entries.bf62e2007620c103df79033af8eb8716acf95c89: 1Ki 15:32 1Ki 15:32 is simply a repetition of 1Ki 15:16; and the remark concerning Baasha’s attitude towards Asa of Judah immediately after his entrance upon the government precedes the account of his reign, for the purpose of indicating at the very outset, that the overthrow of the dynasty of Jeroboam and the rise of a new dynasty did not alter the hostile relation between the kingdom of Israel and the kingdom of Judah.
entries.63feacb43e8238661fe2631e257e8bbc3a283215: 1Ki 15:33-34 <div eID="gen4990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4991" type="x-p"/> The Reign of Baasha is described very briefly according to its duration (two years) and its spirit, namely, the attitude of Baasha towards the Lord (1Ki 15:34); there then follow in 1Ki 16:1-4 the words of the prophet Jehu, the son of Hanani (<reference osisRef="2Chr.16.7">2Ch 16:7</reference>), concerning the extermination of the family of Baasha; and lastly, in 1Ki 16:5-7, his death is related with the standing allusion to the annals of the kings. The words of Jehu concerning Baasha (1Ki 16:1-4) coincide exactly <hi type="italic">mutatis mutandis</hi> with the words of Ahijah concerning Jeroboam.<note placement="foot">“There was something very strange in the perversity and stolidity of the kings of Israel, that when they saw that the families of preceding kings were evidently overthrown by the command of God on account of the worship of the calves, and they themselves had overturned them, they nevertheless worshipped the same calves, and placed them before the people for them to worship, that they might not return to the temple and to Asa, king of Jerusalem; though prophets denounced it and threatened their destruction. Truly the devil and the ambition of reigning blinded them and deprived them of their senses. Hence it came to pass, through the just judgment of God, that they all were executioners of one another in turn: Baasha was the executioner of the sons of Jeroboam; Zambri was the executioner of the sons of Baasha; and the executioner of Zambri was Omri.” -  C. a Lapide.</note> <div eID="gen4991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4992" type="x-p"/> The expression “exalted thee out of the dust,” instead of “from among the people” (1Ki 14:7), leads to the conjecture that Baasha had risen to be king from a very low position. גּבוּרתו (his might) in 1Ki 16:5 refers, as in the case of Asa (1Ki 15:23), less to brave warlike deeds, than generally to the manifestation of strength and energy in his government.  <chapter eID="1Kgs.15"/> <div eID="gen4992" type="x-p"/>

                        <ns0:hi>Obj.</ns0:hi> How can this be, when he Reigned 3 Years, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 2. and <ns0:hi>Asa,</ns0:hi> his Successor, began his Reign in the twentieth Year of <ns0:hi>Ieroboam, v.</ns0:hi> 9? <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> Parts of Years are common<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly called and accounted Years both in the old and New Testa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment, and in prophane Writers. And thus one and the same Year may well be, as it frequently is, attributed to two several Persons.</ns0:note> the son of Nebat, reigned Abijam over Judah.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 Three years <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">See the last Note, on <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 1.</ns0:note> reigned he in Jerusalem: and his mothers name <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> Maachah the daughter of Abishalom <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>of Absalom,</ns0:hi> as he is called 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 11. 21.
